name: Accent training
lead: Accent training, also called accent reduction, accent modification or accent neutralization, is structured study of a language's sounds, stress, rhythm and intonation so that a speaker can be understood more easily or sound closer to a chosen target accent.[1] People who use it for their presentation, rather than only for clarity, treat the voice as part of the overall impression they make: a clearer, more familiar-sounding voice can shape how listeners rate a speaker's competence, polish and likability in interviews, presentations and everyday conversation.[7][9]

It is offered by speech-language pathologists, acting and dialect coaches, and linguists.[1][16] Speech-language pathologists in the United States describe their role as improving intelligibility for unfamiliar listeners, and they do not regard accents or dialects as communication disorders to be treated.[1] Programs typically work on difficult vowels and consonants, word stress, rhythm, linking and speaking rate, and can last from a few days to several months.[1]

Research comes mainly from linguistics and psychology rather than from clinical trials of appearance. Laboratory studies show that listeners adapt to unfamiliar accents with exposure and short training, and that the adaptation can be specific to the accent heard.[2][12] A matched-guise study of 1,699 listeners found that reactions to accented English depended on the communication context, and a 2024 meta-analysis of 139 effect sizes found standard-accented job candidates were rated more hireable than non-standard-accented candidates (d = 0.47).[3][9]

More favourable first impressions in interviews, presentations and conversation
angle.text: People take accent training so that their speech sounds clearer or closer to a prestige or familiar accent, which they expect will improve how they come across in professional and social settings. Actors use the same techniques to adopt accents for roles.

paras: Accent training breaks speech into parts and builds them back up into conversation. For English, programs commonly target sounds that learners from particular first languages find difficult, such as the th sounds, r, l and w, along with vowel contrasts practised through minimal pairs like his/is or hill/ill, plus word stress, rhythm and intonation.[1] Some programs also cover linking between words, speaking rate and voice projection, and finish with conversational practice.[1]

Descriptions of common transfer patterns illustrate how coaches tailor the work. Speakers of Spanish and Portuguese may add an h before the vowel in words such as is, so that it sounds like his, while speakers of some Asian languages may add a y sound before words such as in.[1] Coaches address these patterns with listening discrimination and production drills.

Speech-language pathologists, acting coaches and linguists all offer instruction, in person, in groups or online.[1] Speech-language pathology bodies state that accent modification is an elective service, and that its aim is not to remove a speaker's cultural or linguistic identity but to improve intelligibility for listeners unfamiliar with the accent.[1]

Deliberate accent teaching is older than the modern 'accent reduction' label. Received Pronunciation, the prestige accent of England, grew out of an accent of south-eastern England spread through the universities and fee-charging public schools; Daniel Jones adopted the name in 1926, and the BBC under John Reith adopted educated south-eastern speech as a broadcast standard in 1922.[14] An 1891 teacher's handbook is quoted as holding that educated people should speak so that nobody could tell what county they came from.[14]

In the United States, a consciously learned accent known as Good American Speech, partly shaped by the speech of the Northeastern elite, was used by early twentieth-century actors and announcers and is often called the Mid-Atlantic or transatlantic accent.[17] Prestige has shifted since: from the Second World War, and especially the 1960s, regional accents gained wider acceptance in British education and public life, although surveys from 1969 to 2022 still rank RP as the most prestigious British accent.[14]
A 2007 Los Angeles Times report described a surge in accent-reduction classes among immigrants and others who wanted to sound more American.[1]

sections.h: What accent is and how it is acquired
paras: Accents signal group membership and can reflect region, class or background; General American and Received Pronunciation are sometimes called 'accentless', though everyone speaks with an accent.[15] Researchers describe accents as relatively flexible until the early twenties and more fixed afterwards, although speech continues to change across a lifetime.[15]

Studies of second-language speakers identify age of learning, length of residence, language similarity and frequency of use as factors affecting accent strength, and Flege, Munro and MacKay's 1995 study examined factors affecting strength of perceived foreign accent.[15][18] The critical period hypothesis holds that native-like pronunciation becomes harder to acquire after about puberty; it remains debated, with rare adult learners reported to pass as native speakers.[15]

Linguists distinguish accentedness (how different speech sounds from a reference accent) from intelligibility and comprehensibility (how easily it is understood). Munro and Derwing's 1995 study examined the relationship between processing time, accent and comprehensibility, and later authors argue that intelligibility matters more than a native-like accent for second-language speakers.[13][15]

Linguists describe the outcome as gradual. Dennis Baron, a linguistics professor at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, is quoted as saying that eliminating an accent is difficult and that softening one takes years of interaction with native speakers.[1] Programs therefore commonly describe their goal as greater clarity rather than complete replacement of an accent.[1]

Work on adult learners shows measurable gains from formal courses. In a study of fifty adult Polish speakers of English tested before and after a two-semester accent training course, the English vowels they produced were compared with those of their pronunciation teachers, and pre-existing musical hearing and musical experience related to how successfully the vowels were acquired.[4]

Accent coaches describe working through a hierarchy that moves from sounds to connected speech. Typical elements include listening discrimination, minimal-pair drills, mapping where the tongue, lips and jaw sit for target sounds, and shadowing recordings of a chosen model speaker, followed by conversational practice with feedback.[1] Many providers now deliver this online by video lessons or recorded speech comparison, and apps and software have been developed that give pronunciation feedback; a 2009 paper described foreign-accent conversion in computer-assisted pronunciation training.[1]

Dialect coaches for actors use related techniques. They research real-world voices, curate recordings, give feedback during filming or rehearsal and aim to remove obstacles so that the accent does not distract an audience. On low-budget productions, native-speaker models and self-study archives or standard reading passages such as Comma Gets a Cure may replace a coach.[16]

Perceptual studies explain why training aimed at the listener can matter. In experiments on adaptation to foreign-accented speech, listeners trained on Korean-accented English transcribed new words better than untrained controls, and the benefit was larger when training and test accents matched, which indicates that adaptation is partly specific to each accent.[2] An eye-tracking study found that brief training with a salient artificial accent changed how listeners recognised accented words.[6] A preprint measured listening performance and cognitive load over five days of brief exposure to an unfamiliar accent, reflecting the view that listeners tune to accents with exposure.[5]

A matched-guise experiment with 1,699 German, Spanish and Singaporean listeners compared Dutch-accented English with standard British and American English across a lecture, an audio tour and a job pitch. Dutch-accented English was understood as well as the two native accents and received equally positive or more positive ratings, and the authors concluded that training toward a native accent may not always be necessary for learners who mostly speak with other second-language speakers.[3]

Listeners also benefit from familiarity: a 2014 study of Glasgow and Standard Southern British English listeners found that both long-term familiarity with an accent and short-term familiarization reduced the processing cost of an unfamiliar accent, without removing it entirely.[12]

Wikipedia's accent article cites Gluszek and Dovidio's 2010 review reporting that non-native accents can be stigmatized, with speakers judged as less intelligent, competent or educated, and de la Zerda and Hopper's 1979 study of bias in employment interviews.[15] Wikipedia's linguistic discrimination article summarises research linking certain accents with perceived differences in intelligence, status and likability, with prestige varying by context.[7]

The 2024 meta-analysis by Spence and colleagues combined 139 effect sizes (4,576 participants): standard-accented candidates were more hireable (d = 0.47), the bias was stronger for high-communication jobs, was larger for foreign than regional accents and for female candidates, and was associated with perceived social status rather than relative comprehensibility.[9] A 2013 study found that White and Asian nonnative speakers using the same scripts were less likely to be recommended for a middle-management role, and that the effect was mediated by perceived political skill.[11] A 2024 review describes accent discrimination at work as a topic that has received less attention than visually based diversity categories.[10]

Findings in the other direction also exist: the 2020 matched-guise study found Dutch-accented English was understood as well as standard British and American English and rated equally or more positively by listeners from Germany, Spain and Singapore.[3]

sections.h: Accent training for appearance and presentation
paras: In presentation-focused circles, accent training sits beside voice and speech work such as pitch, pace, articulation and posture-supported breathing, treated as part of how a person comes across. Proponents say clearer pronunciation and a more familiar accent make interviews, public speaking, sales calls and video content easier to follow, while others pursue a particular accent such as General American or RP for style or for acting.[1][16]

The surrounding debate is between providers who describe a voluntary service chosen for personal goals and critics who argue the industry responds to bias rather than addressing it; speech-language pathology bodies state that the aim is not to remove a speaker's cultural or linguistic identity.[1][7]

Linguists describe the outcome as gradual. Dennis Baron of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign is quoted as saying that eliminating an accent is difficult and that softening one takes years of interaction with native speakers.[1] Under US labor law, employers may base decisions on accent where it interferes with the work, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission receives complaints each year from people who believe they faced accent-related discrimination.[1]

A 2011 study of Chinese American adolescents reported that accent, perpetual-foreigner stereotypes and perceived discrimination linked English proficiency with depressive symptoms, showing why some people seek accent change.[19]

No studies found of accent training as an appearance intervention. Related laboratory research on listeners shows that perceptual adaptation to accented speech can be specific to an accent[2] and that musical hearing skills relate to learning second-language English vowels.[4] A 2016 study on second-language learners of Portuguese examined how language experience shapes sound discrimination and noted implications for foreign accent training.[8]

A 2007 Los Angeles Times report described a surge in accent-reduction classes among immigrants and others who wanted to sound more American.[1]Several actors are reported to have trained for American accents for roles, although these reports are listed in Wikipedia as needing sources.[1]

Wikipedia lists Portia de Rossi, Anthony LaPaglia, Katherine Langford and Charlize Theron as people who trained to develop American accents, with those claims tagged as needing citations; dialect coaching is a paid specialty in film and television, with fewer than 100 living film and TV coaches listed on IMDb according to Wikipedia.[1][16]

Under US labor law, employers may base decisions on accent where it interferes with the work, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission receives complaints each year from people who believe they faced accent-related discrimination.[1] Critics of the accent-reduction industry argue that it responds to bias rather than addressing it, while providers say they offer a voluntary service that clients choose for their own goals.[1][7]

lore.intro: Accent training is discussed by coaches, language learners and presentation-minded people as a way to change how the voice is received; claims below reflect what providers and learners say, set against research.[1][9]

claims.claim: A clearer or more standard accent improves first impressions at work
claims.believers: Providers and learners say interviewers and clients respond more favourably to speech that is easy to follow and familiar.[1]
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis found standard-accented candidates rated more hireable (d = 0.47), though comprehensibility did not explain the bias.[9]

claims.claim: You can fully lose an accent with enough coaching
claims.believers: Some programs describe accent neutralization as an achievable goal over weeks or months.[1]
claims.experts: Dennis Baron is quoted as saying eliminating an accent is difficult and softening one takes years; researchers describe accents as more fixed after the early twenties.[1][15]

claims.claim: Accent change is mainly about intelligibility
claims.believers: Speech-language pathology bodies describe the goal as intelligibility for unfamiliar listeners.[1]
claims.experts: A 2020 study found Dutch-accented English was understood as well as British and American English, and the authors said training toward a native accent may not always be necessary.[3]

claims.claim: Listeners get used to accents quickly
claims.believers: Coaches say talking with a speaker for a while makes the accent easier to follow.
claims.experts: Laboratory studies show adaptation with short exposure or training that can be specific to the accent, and 2014 research found familiarization reduced but did not remove processing costs.[2][12]

claims.claim: A musical ear helps with accent learning
claims.believers: Learners with musical backgrounds report picking up sounds faster.
claims.experts: A study of fifty adult Polish speakers found musical hearing and experience related to English vowel acquisition after a two-semester course.[4]

claims.claim: Accent bias is a prejudice rather than a communication issue
claims.believers: Critics of the industry argue that listeners devalue 'otherness' and that training responds to bias.[7][9]
claims.experts: The meta-analysis found bias was associated with perceived social status and not with comprehensibility, consistent with a prejudice explanation, while processing-fluency explanations remain discussed.[9][10]

claims.claim: A British (RP) accent signals intelligence or class
claims.believers: Many people say RP sounds educated or upper class.[14]
claims.experts: Surveys from 1969 to 2022 still rank RP as the most prestigious British accent, but some associate it with privilege and it is disliked in parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland.[14]

card.summary: Coaching to change or clarify an accent; linguists say it takes years, and its appearance value is unstudied.
card.note: Full accent change can take years.

quick.overview:
Accent training teaches the sounds and rhythms of a target accent, usually to improve clarity.

It is offered by speech coaches and linguists; listener research exists but not on appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Practice of target vowels, consonants, stress and intonation with feedback.
quick.risks: No physical harms documented; some linguists warn about unrealistic expectations.
